title: No one wants to go
hookLine: one by one the great disciples decline, each remembering being out-argued by him

cards: The Buddha asks a simple favor: go and ask after Vimalakirti; he's ill. He turns first to Shariputra, the disciple known for wisdom. And Shariputra says, as the sutra tells it: I'm not fit to go.
Then he explains why, with a story about himself coming off badly. The Buddha turns to the next disciple, and the next. Each one says no.
Each one has a story, and every story is told by the one who lost the argument.

teach.b: Here are a few of the stories, paraphrased. Shariputra remembers sitting quietly under a tree in the forest, deep in meditation. Vimalakirti came by and told him: that isn't the way to sit.
Sit without withdrawing from the world. Sit while doing the ordinary things of life, without leaving behind the people around you. Shariputra had no answer, so he stayed silent.
Maudgalyayana remembers teaching a crowd of householders in the street; Vimalakirti stopped him and said the teaching can't be handed out the way he was handing it out.
Mahakashyapa remembers going only to poor houses for alms, to give the poor a chance to earn merit. Vimalakirti told him to beg from everyone alike, rich and poor. And then Ananda.

The Buddha had been unwell, and Ananda went to a house to fetch some milk. Vimalakirti met him at the door: hush, the Buddha's body is the body of the teaching; don't let anyone hear you say he's sick.
Ananda was mortified. Then a voice from the sky said: Ananda, the layman is right. But go and take the milk, and don't be ashamed.
Look at what the sutra is doing.
These are the great disciples, the names at the center of the older discourses, and each one remembers being out-argued by a householder, and says so in front of everyone.
Then even the bodhisattvas decline, Maitreya among them. Each refusal makes the visit sound harder. The sutra is clearing the room for someone.

how: Some teachers in Mahayana traditions use these refusal stories to teach that practice is not limited to the forest or the meditation hall, and that a layperson's insight can match a monk's.

games.q: what does “no one wants to go” mean?
o: the great disciples each refusing to visit Vimalakirti
townspeople staying away from a contagious sickbed
the Buddha refusing to send anyone to a layman

games.q: no one wants to go: tap the pairs.
p: told how to sit under a tree
went to fetch milk for the Buddha
the layman is right, but take the milk

s: the disciples decline because Vimalakirti is contagious
each declines because Vimalakirti once out-argued him.
Ananda is told to take the milk anyway
a voice from the sky says the layman is right, but go, and don't be ashamed.
only the disciples decline, never the bodhisattvas
the bodhisattvas decline too, Maitreya among them.

games.q: you're Shariputra. the Buddha asks you to visit Vimalakirti, the layman who once corrected you while you sat in the forest. what do you do?
o: go gladly, ready for a rematch.
decline, and tell everyone the story of being out-argued.
send a gift instead and say you're busy.
games.why: he says he's not fit to go, and tells the story against himself, in front of everyone. the others do the same.

practice: Let a memory come of someone getting the better of you in a conversation: a sibling, a teacher, a child whose question stumped you. Notice how it sits in the body, maybe a little heat in the face.
Then say to yourself, plainly, as the disciples did: they were right, and I had no answer.

wordCard.voice: No one wants to go. One by one the Buddha's great disciples decline to visit Vimalakirti, each remembering the day he left them speechless. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Shariputra, the disciple known for wisdom, the first to decline.

carryVoice: Your line: they all declined. Someone is still going to knock on that door. Back tomorrow, same hill.
